4. Qg7 is well-formed SAN and illegal in the position reached. Two further legal-looking moves follow it deliberately, so a reader that skipped rather than stopped would produce a longer mainline and fail.

MEASURED, AND THE NUMBER TO LOOK AT IS `plies`. An unclosed `{` swallows the rest of the game — moves 3 and 4 and the result token — and the reader reports complete success: truncatedAtPly is null. Four plies vanish with nothing to indicate it. This is why `plies` is asserted separately: our `Mainline` type can say 'stopped at ply n' but has no way to say 'read to the end of what was left, and what was left was wrong'.

MEASURED: one damaged game becomes TWO games. The unclosed quote in [Event "...] runs on until the next quote, which consumes the following tag lines, and the tokenizer then treats the movetext as a separate game with default headers. Consequences for ADR-0008 rule 7 and B-097: the import report's game count can exceed the number of games in the file, so 'imported 4 of 3' is a reachable state. Also relevant to rule 6, since a split game hashes as neither half.

MEASURED: chessops FILLS IN the five missing roster tags with defaults — Event becomes "?", Result becomes "*" — so the header map always holds seven entries and the reader cannot distinguish a missing tag from a tag whose value is literally "?". A real value: the importer must decide disposition from the bytes, not from the parser's header map.

Result appears twice (1-0 then 0-1) and Date twice. MEASURED: chessops keeps the FIRST occurrence. Nothing says pgn-reader must agree, and if it keeps the last, the same file yields a different result in Rust and TypeScript from a file neither considers broken — B-064 divergence with no illegal move anywhere in sight. Worth asserting on both sides for exactly that reason.

MEASURED, and it is not what the file says: the tag reads [Result "1-0"], the movetext ends 0-1, and chessops reports Result as 0-1. The game-termination token overwrites the header. So 'derive the hot fields from the tags' is not sufficient on its own — the token can silently win, and ADR-0005's derived `result` column depends on which source we mean. Rule 2 says repair is to derived values only, and this is a case where a repair happens whether we ask for one or not.

A complete roster and no moves. NOT quarantined: ADR-0008 reserves that for bytes with no movetext AND no recognisable tag pair, and this has seven of them. A real crosstab row rather than an error — a scheduled-but-unplayed game looks exactly like this.

A PNG signature plus random bytes, named .pgn. MEASURED: this does not throw and does not produce zero games — it produces ONE game with seven default headers and no moves, which is indistinguishable from headers-without-moves.pgn if you only look at the parse result. The two fixtures sit next to each other on purpose: telling them apart requires asking whether any literal tag pair existed in the bytes, which is precisely how ADR-0008 words the quarantine test.

Player names carrying umlauts and accents, encoded Latin-1, with nothing in the file declaring it. Decoded as UTF-8 the names come back with U+FFFD replacement characters while the MOVES parse perfectly — so the game looks fine and the people in it are quietly corrupted. That is rule 5's whole justification, and it lands downstream in B-058's name normalisation rather than anywhere visible.

THE MOST IMPORTANT MEASUREMENT IN THIS CORPUS, and it is worse than ADR-0008 rule 4 describes. 2. Sf3 (Springer, knight) does not fail — chessops's PGN TOKENIZER drops the unrecognised piece letter and yields the SAN `f3`, which is a legal pawn move. Same for Sc6 -> c6. So the derived game becomes 1. e4 e5 2. f3 c6, a real game that was never played, with no warning of any kind; only 3. Lb5 finally fails and truncates. Rule 4 argued that legality cannot arbitrate between notation languages because of the R/roi collision. Measured, the situation is worse: the corruption happens at tokenization, BEFORE legality is consulted, and `node.san` no longer contains the file's own text — so a warning cannot be derived by comparing our SAN against the source without re-reading the raw bytes.

The same failure through a different convention: 2. Cf3 (cavalier) becomes f3, Cc6 becomes c6, and 3. Fb5 truncates. Two fixtures rather than one because rule 4's required implementation is to scan a whole file for letters unique to one convention — S/L/T for German, C/F for French — so the corpus needs an example of each to test the scan rather than a single hardcoded letter.

The R/roi collision made concrete, and it is silent by construction. White has Ke1 and Ra1, both of which can legally reach d1, so `Rd1` is a legal rook move under the English reading and a legal KING move under the French one. MEASURED: chessops plays the rook (final position has R on d1, K still on e1) with no complaint. Legality genuinely cannot arbitrate here — there is nothing wrong to detect, only two valid readings of the same text, which is why rule 4 decides notation language per file from unambiguous evidence and never per token.

This fixture rewrote rule 3b (B-113, addendum accepted session 5), so the disposition here is the AMENDED one: a supported variant whose moves are legal under its own rules is `clean`, exactly like a standard game. MEASURED: chessops's startingPosition() reads the Variant tag and returns a Crazyhouse position, so the mainline derives correctly — pocket in the FEN, drop `P@e4` played as a drop. The original rule assumed a useless 'illegal move at ply 2' here and would have had the importer derive nothing for a game the UI plays through in full. The premise turned out to be true of Rust and false of TypeScript: shakmaty requires the caller to choose a variant, chessops reads the tag. Two libraries, opposite defaults, same tag — the B-064 category, which the old rule would have frozen into the specification.

The branch where rule 3b genuinely earns its place: a Variant tag naming something chessops does not implement ("Grand Chess") makes startingPosition() return ERR_VARIANT, which our reader surfaces as truncatedAtPly 0 — the same value it uses for an unparseable FEN. So 'this is a variant we do not support' and 'this position is garbage' are currently the same observable, which is exactly the misdiagnosis rule 3b was written to prevent, just arriving through a different door than the ADR expected.

MEASURED: [Variant "Fischerandom"] silently maps to standard chess and the standard starting position, so a Chess960 game with no FEN header derives a plausible, wrong mainline with no error. Quieter than the unknown-variant case and harder to notice, because everything succeeds. Chess960 exports normally carry SetUp/FEN, which is what saves this in practice — but 'normally' is doing the work in that sentence.

Half of the rule 6 pair. POST-MVP SPECIFICATION: rule 6 was removed from the MVP by the session-5 addendum — nothing hashes a game any more, because dedupe protects against re-importing one file twice, which is not what ADR-0004's derivability condition needs. Kept in the corpus because these two files are the evidence for whenever dedupe is designed (B-022). Ten tags, per-move { [%clk] } comments, movetext wrapped across three lines, LF endings.

The same game re-exported: seven tags instead of ten, clock comments stripped, different line wrapping, CRLF endings, result token on its own line. Byte-different in every respect a naive hash would notice, identical in players, event, date, round, result and moves. Whenever dedupe is built (B-022), a key over the normalised game must merge these two and a key over the bytes must not — and it must include the variant, which the Seven Tag Roster does not carry. That hole is why the rule got re-examined at all, and the better answer was to delete the mechanism from the MVP rather than patch the key.
